catalog_quote: The simplest generalization that can be made is that word-level stress is assigned to the strongest syllable in the PrWd, if there is only one. [p. 58] ... The only exception to the STRONGEST generalization is that light ultimas (CV, CVN) are not stressed. ... In general, when two or more syllables tie for strongest in a PrWd, the rightmost is stressed, excluding a light ultima (21). ... establishing a four-step weight scale based on syllable structure alone: CVVN ⮎ CVV ⮎ CVN ⮎ CV. [p. 59] ... Word-level stress is assigned to the rightmost strongest syllable in the PrWd. The scale that grades syllables for word stress overlaps almost completely with the foot-level Strength scale. The difference is that for word stress, vowel quality is more important than whether or not a coda is present. [p. 66] ... a light ultima is not stressed, even when it is the strongest syllable in the PrWd: No-Final-Stress ⮎ QualPW. However, a heavy ultima does receive word stress when it is the strongest syllable in the word: Quant ⮎ No-Final-Stress. Finally, when more than one syllable in a PrWd is eligible for word stress (based on Strength), word stress falls on the rightmost, but not if this would require parsing a foot at the right edge of the PrWd: No-Final-Foot ⮎ Rightmost. [p. 67]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Prominence-driven, weight/quality-sensitive system with an iambic default: the prosodic word (excluding extraprosodic object/modal suffixes) is parsed left-to-right into disyllabic feet, iambic unless a stronger syllable pulls stress; primary (word-level) stress goes to the strongest syllable on a multigrade scale (quantity CVVN > CVV > CVN > CV; vowel height a > e,o > i; diphthong > monophthong; closed > open), and if several syllables tie, to the rightmost of them; a light final syllable (CV, CVN) is never stressed, but a heavy CVV/CVVN ultima that is the strongest syllable does take main stress (p. 62). Michael 2008 (pp. 231-234) adds that nouns use the simpler iambic L-to-R parse with final extrametricality and rightmost primary stress, ignoring vowel quality, and often carry lexical stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes, described in detail: iterative left-to-right disyllabic feet, iambic by default, with foot-level (secondary) stress also sensitive to the strength scale (Quant > Qual > Rhythm), stress-clash avoidance, and iambic-to-trochaic shift when the left syllable of a foot is stronger (C&M 2005 §3, pp. 50-57; Michael 2008 p. 232).
new_statements.exceptions: Heavy (CVV, CVVN) ultimas regularly take primary stress when strongest (p. 62); the rightmost strongest syllable is skipped if stressing it would require a word-final foot (No-Final-Foot > Rightmost, pp. 63-64, 67); word-final foot allowed only to reach the strongest syllable; nouns (per Michael 2008) are insensitive to vowel quality and show widespread lexical stress, e.g. lexicalised gender suffixes -ri/-ro behaving as extraprosodic; reflexive pronouns have lexically specified leftmost stress (Michael 2008).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the prosodic word minus 'metrically inert' (extraprosodic) suffixes/clitics (object person markers, subordinator -ra, counterfactual -me), so the rightmost stress can sit up to six syllables from the end of the morphological word (p. 49-50). Phrase-final words and, for some speakers, citation forms take a PHRASAL stress on the penultimate syllable that overrides the word-level pattern; the authors therefore used only non-phrase-final words from recorded texts (p. 48). Transcriptions are impressionistic, checked against spectrograms where necessary.
new_statements.identity_note: Both saved sources describe the Nanti of the Camisea headwaters communities (Montetoni, Marankehari), i.e. Glottolog nant1250 proper; no dialect split. Caveat from Michael 2008 (p. 231): stress assignment differs by word class — the Crowhurst & Michael 2005 generalisation (all examples are verb forms) is the verbal system; nouns are parsed by the same left-to-right iambic feet with final-syllable extrametricality and rightmost primary stress but are insensitive to vowel quality and show widespread lexical stress.

new_statements.quote: Nanti possesses a typologically very unusual stress-system. Specifically, stress assignment in Nanti words overwhelmingly depends on syllable prominence, which arises from nuclear sonority, rather than on syllable position, which is the vastly more typologically common criterion for stress assignment. [...] Unlike the other sonority-driven stress systems described in the literature, however, the Nanti stress system is iterative (i.e. involves multiple feet per prosodic word) [pp. 166-167] [...] in Nanti, words are footed by bisyllabic feet that are formed from left to right, with the final syllable always left unfooted, unless it incorporates a long vowel or diphthong. [p. 19]

new_statements.relation_note: Same system as the existing Crowhurst & Michael 2005 statement (iterative footing, final light syllable never stressed, prominence/sonority decides stress within the foot): sonority-driven iterative stress, weight-sensitive. It is an earlier, less detailed statement by the same author and adds nothing beyond the 2005 article; the catalog's rule field is currently empty, so this fills it rather than changing it.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is assigned iteratively: words are parsed into bisyllabic feet from left to right, the final syllable stays unfooted (so unstressed) unless it contains a long vowel or diphthong, and within each foot the stressed syllable is chosen by syllable prominence (nuclear sonority: vowel quality, length, diphthongs) rather than by fixed position. The author calls it a sonority-driven, iterative stress system (citing Kenstowicz 1994).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Implied by the iterative footing ('multiple feet per prosodic word'), but the thesis does not distinguish primary from secondary stress or say which foot carries the main stress.
new_statements.exceptions: The section mentions stress-clash sensitivity that can produce 'domino-like shifting of stresses in a word' and degenerate feet formed only under conditions involving the relative prominence of neighbouring syllables; footnote 63 says the main features are shared by other Kampa languages (J. Payne 1991). No worked examples are given; the appendix is a two-paragraph summary.
new_statements.identity_note: The thesis is based on fieldwork 1995-2001 in the Nanti communities of Montetoni and Maranxejari (Camisea River, Peru); it is the same variety as Crowhurst & Michael 2005. Footnote 63 notes that the main features are shared with other Kampa languages (citing J. Payne 1991 on Asheninka).
